finding.claim: Shared access can never be revoked: there is no unshare, remove or delete route, so once a user is appended to the shared list they keep read access (including future edits) for the note's lifetime, and the owner cannot revoke a former or compromised collaborator.
finding.source: Owner-authenticated POST /n/<nid>/share with a 'user' value in the JSON body (notes.py:41-45)
finding.sink: n["shared"].append(...) at notes.py:45, which grants read access via can_view (notes.py:8) and require_view (notes.py:28)

trace.note: require_edit ensures only the owner can share
request.json['user'] appended to note['shared'] with no removal path
can_view returns True for any user in note['shared'], indefinitely
read route calls require_view, which admits the revoked-in-intent user

finding.guards_checked: require_edit (notes.py:44) restricts granting to the owner; shared users cannot re-share or write (can_edit at notes.py:16-17). No unshare, delete or expiry route or check exists anywhere in notes.py (routes only at lines 25, 32, 41).

verdict.guard_found: require_edit at notes.py:20-22 (via require_edit call at notes.py:44) restricts granting to the owner, and can_edit at notes.py:16-17 denies shared users write access. The trace lines all match the file: route at :41, owner check at :44, append at :45, can_view at :8, require_view at :28.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate, but the claim describes a missing revocation feature rather than an authorization bypass: the only party who can add a user to notes.py:45 is the owner, enforced by require_edit at notes.py:44, so every retained grant is one the owner deliberately made. An attacker would need to be the owner (or an account that already holds owner power), and nothing in the file shows that the owner's inability to revoke gives an unauthorized party access. At most this is a functional gap (no unshare route, as the file has only routes at lines 25, 32, 41), not a vulnerability.

finding.claim: Note-ID existence oracle: NOTES[nid] is a bare dict lookup performed before any authorization check, so a missing ID yields KeyError (HTTP 500) while an existing but unauthorized ID yields 403, letting any authenticated user enumerate valid note IDs.
finding.source: Any authenticated request to /n/<nid> (read), PUT /n/<nid> (write), or POST /n/<nid>/share with an attacker-chosen nid
finding.sink: Differential response: KeyError from NOTES[nid] (notes.py:27, :34, :43) versus abort(403) from require_view/require_edit/can_edit (notes.py:13, :22, :36)

trace.note: n = NOTES[nid] raises KeyError for unknown nid before any check
require_view runs only after successful lookup
abort(403) for existing note the caller cannot view

finding.guards_checked: Authorization checks (require_view notes.py:28, can_edit notes.py:35, require_edit notes.py:44) run only after the lookup, so they do not hide existence. Exploitability depends on how note IDs are generated, which is not in this repository.

verdict.guard_found: none. No before_request hook, errorhandler, or try/except in notes.py maps KeyError to 404 or hides it. The authorization checks (require_view notes.py:28, can_edit notes.py:35, require_edit notes.py:44) all run after the bare lookup at notes.py:27, :34, and :43, so they cannot prevent the differential.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches: NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27/34/43 raises KeyError before require_view/can_edit/require_edit, which abort(403) at notes.py:13/22/36 for an existing note the caller cannot access, so a missing ID (500) and an unauthorized existing ID (403) are distinguishable. The attacker is any authenticated user, since g.user is set outside this repo, and that is the only caveat: the practical impact depends on how note IDs are generated (e.g. high-entropy IDs make enumeration impractical), which the repo does not show.

finding.claim: Unbounded, non-deduplicated and unvalidated shared list: the owner can repeatedly append the same or non-string values (dicts, lists) with no type check, dedupe or size cap, growing the list without bound, slowing every can_view scan, and injecting arbitrary JSON into every read response. No body size limit is set in this file.
finding.source: Owner's JSON body on POST /n/<nid>/share ('user' field, notes.py:45) and PUT /n/<nid> ('body' field, notes.py:37)
finding.sink: n["shared"].append(...) at notes.py:45; linear scan in can_view (notes.py:8); serialization via jsonify(n) (notes.py:29)

trace.note: request.json['user'] appended with no type validation or dedupe
user in note['shared'] performs linear scan on every access check
jsonify(n) serializes the stored non-string values into read responses
request.json['body'] stored with no size limit in this file

finding.guards_checked: Owner-only sharing (require_edit notes.py:44). Impact is largely self-affecting to the owner's own note; no MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH or schema validation is configured in this file.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22, called at notes.py:44) calls abort(403) unless g.user is the owner, so only the note owner reaches notes.py:45. Also can_edit (notes.py:16-17) and the owner check in write (notes.py:35-36).
verdict.reason: All four trace lines (notes.py:8, 29, 37, 45) match the claim, but the only caller that can reach notes.py:45 is the note owner, enforced by require_edit at notes.py:44 with abort(403) at notes.py:22. The owner already has full write control over the note body (notes.py:37), so growing its own shared list only affects the owner's own note and grants no new power, which makes this a self-inflicted issue rather than a vulnerability.

finding.claim: Read responses expose the full note record, including the owner identity and the complete shared collaborator roster, to any user admitted by can_view, including read-only shared collaborators.
finding.source: Any shared collaborator (user in note['shared']) issuing GET /n/<nid>
finding.sink: jsonify(n) at notes.py:29 returning owner and shared fields

trace.note: require_view admits owner or shared users
jsonify(n) returns the entire record including 'shared' and 'owner'

finding.guards_checked: Read access gated by require_view (notes.py:28) and can_view (notes.py:8). No field projection or redaction of the shared roster for non-owner viewers. Whether this is a leak depends on product intent, which the repository does not document.

verdict.guard_found: require_view (notes.py:11-13) calls can_view (notes.py:7-8) and aborts with 403 when it returns False. The result is tested, not discarded. No field projection or redaction exists between jsonify(n) (notes.py:29) and the response.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: GET /n/<nid> at notes.py:25-29 admits owner and shared users through require_view (notes.py:11-13), and jsonify(n) at notes.py:29 returns the whole record, including owner and shared. Shared collaborators are the intended readers, so the only open question is whether exposing the owner and roster to them is a leak. That depends on product intent, which the repository does not document, so I cannot decide it from the code.
